title: Primes & Sieve of Eratosthenes
description: Test a single number for primality, and find all primes up to n with the sieve

blocks.text: Primes are the atoms of the integers, and problems about them are everywhere. Two questions come up again and again: is this one number prime, and what are all the primes up to some limit?
This topic answers both, with the fast square root test for a single number and the classic Sieve of Eratosthenes for finding many primes at once.
A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself. The first few are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13.
Everything else greater than 1 is composite, meaning it has a smaller divisor. Remember the two special cases: 1 is not prime, and 2 is the only even prime.

To test if n is prime, we only need to look for a divisor up to the square root of n. If no number in that range divides n, it is prime, because any factor larger than the square root would pair with a smaller one we already checked.
This is O(sqrt n) per number, which is fast enough when you only test a few values.
When you need every prime up to some limit n, testing each number one by one is wasteful. The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds them all together, far faster.

blocks.caption: Take the next unmarked number as prime, cross out all its multiples, and repeat

blocks.text: The idea: start with all numbers assumed prime. Take the smallest unmarked number, mark it prime, and cross out every multiple of it. Move to the next unmarked number and repeat. Whatever survives is prime.

Small optimisation:

When crossing out multiples of p, you can start at p times p, because every smaller multiple was already crossed out by a smaller prime.
The sieve is a boolean array and two nested loops.
The right tool depends on how many numbers you must test.

blocks.caption: Trial division for a few numbers, the sieve when you need all primes up to n

items: Testing one or a handful of numbers: use the square root check.
Needing all primes up to n, or many primality queries in that range: build a sieve once.
The sieve runs in about O(n log log n) time and uses O(n) memory.

blocks.text: Prime tools feed many other techniques.

items: Prime factorization, which relies on knowing primes
Number theory problems about coprime pairs
Precomputing primes to speed up repeated queries

blocks.text: The sieve in particular is a precomputation you will reuse across a whole set of problems.
